reading.body:
Earl Flood is named on 65 AI lobbying filings, spread across 25 clients and one firm, with no single client accounting for more than three filings.

The pattern is breadth rather than depth. Every client appears on one, two, or three filings, and the client list runs from chipmakers and cloud-adjacent hardware to hospitals, insurers, retailers, a housing nonprofit, and an electric utility trade group. A lobbyist with this many clients and this few filings per client is carrying a portfolio, not running a single campaign. The three bills named, HR 7757, S 3062, and HR 6875, are the only legislative vehicles the data attaches to him.

For AI specifically, the client mix is the useful signal. Advanced Micro Devices, Marvell, IBM, Scale AI, ElevenLabs, and Palo Alto Networks sit on the same list as Mayo Clinic, HCA, Kaiser, Medtronic, Walmart, and the Edison Electric Institute. That is the shape of AI policy work that has moved past research and into deployment: data center hardware, model developers, and the regulated industries that buy from them. The Edison Electric Institute is the one entry that touches power directly, and it appears at the same three-filing weight as everything else.

What the data does not show is money, timing, or outcome. It records that filings name him, not what was lobbied for, what was spent, or what changed. The prior government positions listed, deputy chief of staff and health policy advisor roles in House and Senate offices, are disclosed under the Lobbying Disclosure Act's twenty-year rule and are not evidence of any particular result. The page also notes a different lobbyist shares the name, so counts should not be merged.
